# Book III, Proposition 6

*Circles touching one another do not have the same centre*

> If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/06-idea.svg" alt="Two circles that touch one another (red, blue) cannot have the same centre: drawn about one centre, the smaller (dashed) lies wholly inside the larger and never touches it." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Two circles that touch one another (red, blue) cannot have the same centre: drawn about one centre, the smaller (dashed) lies wholly inside the larger and never touches it.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/06.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.6, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let the two circles ABC, CDE touch one another at the point C;

I say that they will not have the same centre.

For, if possible, let it be F; let FC be joined, and let FEB be drawn through at random.

Then, since the point F is the centre of the circle ABC,

FC is equal to FB.

Again, since the point F is the centre of the circle CDE,

FC is equal to FE.

But FC was proved equal to FB;

therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop06.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop06.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre. -/
theorem Prop6 {C F : Point} {ABC CDE : Circle} (htouch : CirclesTouch ABC CDE C) :
    ¬ (Centre F ABC ∧ Centre F CDE) := by
  -- For let the two circles ABC, CDE touch one another at the point C;
  have hC : OnCircle C ABC ∧ OnCircle C CDE := by
    rcases htouch with ⟨h₁, h₂, -⟩ | ⟨h₂, h₁, -⟩ | ⟨h₁, h₂, -⟩ <;> exact ⟨h₁, h₂⟩
  -- I say that they will not have the same centre.
  -- For, if possible, let it be F; let FC be joined, and let FEB be drawn through at random.
  rintro ⟨hF₁, hF₂⟩
  obtain ⟨X, hX⟩ := exists_point [F]
  have hXF : X ≠ F := fun h => hX (h ▸ List.mem_singleton_self F)
  obtain ⟨L, hF_L, hX_L⟩ := Postulate1 F X hXF.symm
  obtain ⟨B, hB, hB_L, hBFX⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hF₁) hF_L hX_L hXF
  obtain ⟨E, hE, hE_L, hEFX⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hF₂) hF_L hX_L hXF
  -- Then, since the point F is the centre of the circle ABC,
  -- FC is equal to FB.
  have hFB : ‖F C‖ = ‖F B‖ := Definition15 hF₁ hC.1 hB
  -- Again, since the point F is the centre of the circle CDE,
  -- FC is equal to FE.
  have hFE : ‖F C‖ = ‖F E‖ := Definition15 hF₂ hC.2 hE
  -- But FC was proved equal to FB;
  -- therefore FE is also equal to FB, the less to the greater: which is impossible.
  have hEB : ‖F E‖ = ‖F B‖ := hFE.symm.trans hFB
  /- A common centre and equal radii make one circle (System E, Diagram-segment 2).
     Contact within requires two circles; contact without forbids a point within both. -/
  have hsame : CDE = ABC := circle_eq hF₂ hF₁ hE hB hEB
  subst hsame
  rcases htouch with ⟨-, -, hne, -⟩ | ⟨-, -, hne, -⟩ | ⟨-, -, hout⟩
  · exact hne rfl
  · exact hne rfl
  · exact hout F (centre_inside hF₁) (centre_inside hF₁)
  -- Therefore F is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDE.
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**One look along one straight line.** Euclid supposes that two touching circles have one centre, F, and lets the point of contact, C, settle it. FC is a radius of both circles. A straight line drawn from F at random, FEB, reaches the inner circle at E before the outer at B, and yet FE and FB would each be equal to FC: "the less to the greater: which is impossible".

**"To the intelligence of the reader."** Euclid's figure shows the circles touching within, and the English editions say "internally" in the enunciation, a word Heath calls an interpolation. The fact is, he writes, that "in his usual manner, he chose for demonstration the more difficult case, and left the other case (that of *external* contact) to the intelligence of the reader. It is indeed sufficiently self-evident that circles touching externally cannot have the same centre; but Euclid's proof can really be used for this case too" (vol. 2, p. 13). We take him at his word: our statement covers circles touching within, whichever is the inner, and circles touching without.

**Must E and B be two points?** J. G. Camerer thought the proof takes for granted what Euclid proves only in III.13, that circles touching within at C meet nowhere else. Heath answers that "it is only necessary that *one* line drawn from the assumed common centre should meet the circles in different points" (vol. 2, p. 13), and the very idea of touching within gives one: before the inner circle meets the outer, it has passed through points within it.

**A centre and a radius make one circle.** In Lean the last step goes another way, and Camerer's worry never arises. The rule `circle_eq` (System E, Diagram-segment 2) says that a centre and a radius fix a circle, so FE equal to FB makes the two circles one, whether or not E and B are two points. Lean reads Definition III.3 of the whole circle, as III.11 explains, and the definition closes each case: circles touching within are two circles, and circles touching without have no point within both, though the common centre would be such a point.

**The modern way.** Circles of radii R and r that touch have their centres R + r apart if they touch without, and |R − r| apart if they touch within, where R ≠ r, since two circles of one radius cannot touch within. Neither distance is zero, so the centres differ.
